tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:

content.content:
1	# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 2: Asset Tokenisation and Compliance
2	
3	## Project Context
4	
5	We are developing a decentralised application (dApp) titled **Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum** for the NTU SC4053 Blockchain Technology Development Project.
6	
7	The application simulates an institutional real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation platform, inspired by financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC.
8	
9	Users will eventually be able to create tokenised assets, purchase tokens using testnet ETH, manage investor permissions, and transfer tokens between eligible wallets.
10	
11	The project is being developed in six sequential phases:
12	
13	1. Project Foundation and Architecture — COMPLETED
14	2. Asset Tokenisation and Compliance — CURRENT PHASE
15	3. Asset Registry and Primary Issuance
16	4. Frontend and MetaMask Integration
17	5. End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment
18	6. Security Audit, AI Evaluation and Final Submission
19	
20	**Your task is to fully implement Phase 2, including Solidity development, automated testing, validation, and technical documentation.**
21	
22	Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Step 1: Inspect the Existing Repository
27	
28	Before writing any code:
29	
30	1. Read the existing README, project specifications, architecture documents, and relevant source files.
31	2. Inspect the Hardhat configuration, Solidity compiler version, OpenZeppelin version, package dependencies, and testing framework.
32	3. Understand the architecture established in Phase 1.
33	4. Identify any existing smart contracts or tests relevant to Phase 2.
34	5. Run the existing baseline tests, if available.
35	6. Preserve working Phase 1 code and established project conventions.
36	
37	If there are minor differences between this prompt and the existing repository architecture, adapt the implementation to preserve compatibility. Document any meaningful architectural decisions.
38	
39	Do not unnecessarily reinstall dependencies, overwrite configurations, introduce new frameworks, or restructure the project.
40	
41	## Step 2: Implement `AssetToken.sol`
42	
43	Create or complete:
44	
45	`contracts/AssetToken.sol`
46	
47	This is the core token contract representing fractional interests in a simulated real-world or digital asset.
48	
49	### 2.1 ERC-20 Implementation
50	
51	Use OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 implementation rather than writing token accounting from scratch.
52	
53	The contract must support:
54	
55	- Token name and symbol.
56	- Fixed initial token supply.
57	- Token balances.
58	- Standard `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom` functionality.
59	- ERC-20 `Transfer` and `Approval` events.
60	- Ownership records derived from token balances.
61	
62	The contract constructor should accept:
63	
64	```solidity
65	constructor(
66	    string memory name_,
67	    string memory symbol_,
68	    uint256 initialSupply_,
69	    address issuer_
70	)
71	```
72	
73	Expected behaviour:
74	
75	- The token name and symbol are configured at deployment.
76	- `initialSupply_` is minted to the issuer's wallet.
77	- `totalSupply()` returns the correct fixed supply.
78	- `balanceOf(issuer_)` initially equals `initialSupply_`.
79	- Token decimals are set to **0**, representing whole asset units.
80	- Further minting is not permitted after deployment.
81	- Zero issuer addresses and zero initial supply must be rejected.
82	
83	For example:
84	
85	```text
86	Token Name: Campus Property Token
87	Symbol: CPT
88	Initial Supply: 10,000
89	Decimals: 0
90	
91	Issuer Balance: 10,000 CPT
92	Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
93	```
94	
95	The MVP uses whole token units. Do not automatically multiply the supply by 10^18.
96	
97	### 2.2 Role-Based Access Control
98	
99	Implement role-based permissions using OpenZeppelin AccessControl.
100	
101	At minimum, define:
102	
103	```solidity
104	bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE =
105	    keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE");
106	```
107	
108	The issuer supplied during deployment should initially receive:
109	
110	- `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`
111	- `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`
112	
113	The issuer must also automatically be whitelisted.
114	
115	Only authorised compliance administrators may approve or revoke investor eligibility.
116	
117	Important implementation detail: **Do not assume `msg.sender` is always the issuer during construction.**
118	
119	In Phase 3, the token contract may be deployed by an asset factory on behalf of an issuer. Therefore, roles must be explicitly assigned to the `issuer_` constructor argument rather than blindly assigned to the deploying contract.
120	
121	Do not implement the platform-wide issuer approval system yet; that belongs to Phase 3.
122	
123	### 2.3 Investor Whitelisting
124	
125	Implement an on-chain investor eligibility registry.
126	
127	Suggested state variable:
128	
129	```solidity
130	mapping(address => bool) public isWhitelisted;
131	```
132	
133	Required function:
134	
135	```solidity
136	function setWhitelisted(
137	    address investor,
138	    bool approved
139	) external;
140	```
141	
142	Requirements:
143	
144	1. Only addresses holding `COMPLIANCE_ROLE` may call the function.
145	2. Setting `approved = true` adds an investor to the whitelist.
146	3. Setting `approved = false` revokes an investor's eligibility.
147	4. Zero addresses cannot be whitelisted.
148	5. Emit a `WhitelistUpdated` event when eligibility changes.
149	6. Whitelist status must be publicly readable.
150	
151	An approved investor is permitted to hold and receive the asset tokens.
152	
153	An investor removed from the whitelist must no longer be able to send or receive tokens, even if they still have a positive token balance.
154	
155	Do not forcibly confiscate or burn tokens when whitelist access is revoked.
156	
157	### 2.4 Enforce Transfer Restrictions
158	
159	This is the most important functionality of Phase 2.
160	
161	Modify ERC-20 transfer behaviour so that tokens can only move between whitelisted addresses.
162	
163	Expected behaviour:
164	
165	| Sender | Recipient | Result |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| Whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer succeeds |
168	| Whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
169	| Not whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
170	| Not whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
171	
172	**The restrictions must be enforced inside the token contract itself, not just in a separate purchasing contract or frontend.**
173	
174	Both `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` must respect the restrictions.
175	
176	If OpenZeppelin Contracts v5 is installed, use the appropriate ERC-20 `_update()` override to enforce transfer eligibility. If an older compatible version is already used by the project, implement the equivalent restriction using the supported hook for that version.
177	
178	Do not downgrade OpenZeppelin or use deprecated methods just to follow an example.
179	
180	Handle the zero-address minting case correctly during initial deployment.
181	
182	The initial mint must succeed even though the zero address is not an eligible investor.
183	
184	Avoid adding unnecessary restrictions to standard ERC-20 approval functionality unless required for security.
185	
186	### 2.5 Contract Events and Errors
187	
188	Implement clear events for compliance operations, such as:
189	
190	```solidity
191	event WhitelistUpdated(
192	    address indexed investor,
193	    bool approved,
194	    address indexed operator
195	);
196	```
197	
198	Use descriptive custom errors where appropriate.
199	
200	The code should clearly distinguish failures caused by:
201	
202	- Unauthorised compliance administration.
203	- Invalid wallet addresses.
204	- Non-whitelisted senders.
205	- Non-whitelisted recipients.
206	- Invalid constructor parameters.
207	
208	Keep the implementation concise and readable.
209	
210	### 2.6 Future Compatibility
211	
212	The contract must be designed to support Phase 3 without major redesign.
213	
214	In Phase 3, an `AssetSale` contract will temporarily hold token inventory and distribute tokens to approved investors.
215	
216	Therefore:
217	
218	- Compliance administrators must be able to whitelist smart-contract addresses, not only externally owned wallets.
219	- Whitelisted sale contracts must be capable of receiving and transferring asset tokens.
220	- The token should work when instantiated by a factory contract.
221	- The token must not depend on any frontend implementation.
222	- Each deployed token must maintain independent balances, roles, and whitelist state.
223	
224	Do not implement `AssetSale.sol` or `AssetFactory.sol` in this phase.
225	
226	---
227	
228	## Step 3: Implement Automated Unit Tests
229	
230	Create or update:
231	
232	`test/AssetToken.test.js`
233	
234	Use the testing framework already configured in Phase 1.
235	
236	Tests must be deterministic and must not require Sepolia, MetaMask, live network access, or real ETH.
237	
238	Use multiple local test accounts:
239	
240	```text
241	Account A: Issuer / Compliance Admin
242	Account B: Approved Investor 1
243	Account C: Approved Investor 2
244	Account D: Unapproved Investor
245	Account E: Unauthorised Administrator
246	```
247	
248	### Test Group A — Token Deployment
249	
250	Verify:
251	
252	1. Correct token name.
253	2. Correct token symbol.
254	3. Decimals equal 0.
255	4. Initial total supply equals 10,000.
256	5. Issuer initially receives 10,000 tokens.
257	6. Issuer is automatically whitelisted.
258	7. Issuer receives the required administrator roles.
259	8. Invalid issuer addresses are rejected.
260	9. Zero supply is rejected.
261	10. No externally accessible function can arbitrarily mint additional tokens.
262	
263	### Test Group B — Investor Whitelisting
264	
265	Verify:
266	
267	1. Compliance admin can whitelist Account B.
268	2. Compliance admin can whitelist Account C.
269	3. Approved addresses return `true` from the whitelist.
270	4. Compliance admin can revoke Account B.
271	5. Revoked addresses return `false`.
272	6. Unauthorised Account E cannot whitelist investors.
273	7. Unauthorised Account E cannot revoke investors.
274	8. Whitelist modifications emit the expected event.
275	9. Attempts to whitelist the zero address revert.
276	10. Revoking a wallet does not silently change its token balance.
277	
278	### Test Group C — ERC-20 Transfers
279	
280	Test the following sequence:
281	
282	1. Deploy CPT with 10,000 tokens.
283	2. Whitelist Account B.
284	3. Transfer 100 CPT from issuer to Account B.
285	4. Verify issuer balance equals 9,900.
286	5. Verify Account B balance equals 100.
287	6. Attempt transferring tokens from Account B to unapproved Account D.
288	7. Confirm the transaction reverts.
289	8. Verify all token balances remain unchanged after the revert.
290	9. Whitelist Account C.
291	10. Transfer 20 CPT from Account B to Account C.
292	11. Verify Account B now holds 80 CPT.
293	12. Verify Account C now holds 20 CPT.
294	13. Revoke Account B's whitelist status.
295	14. Verify Account B can neither send nor receive tokens.
296	15. Reapprove Account B.
297	16. Confirm transfers become possible again.
298	
299	### Test Group D — Delegated Transfers
300	
301	Test `approve()` and `transferFrom()`.
302	
303	Verify:
304	
305	- Allowances are created correctly.
306	- An approved delegated transfer between whitelisted holders succeeds.
307	- Delegated transfers to non-whitelisted recipients revert.
308	- Delegated transfers from non-whitelisted token holders revert.
309	- Failed delegated transfers do not unexpectedly alter balances or allowances.
310	- Standard ERC-20 insufficient-allowance behaviour is preserved.
311	
312	Be careful not to confuse the spender with the actual token sender. Compliance checks must cover the token holder (`from`) and recipient (`to`).
313	
314	### Test Group E — Edge Cases
315	
316	Include tests for:
317	
318	- Transfers exceeding the sender's balance.
319	- Transfers of zero tokens.
320	- Transfers to the zero address.
321	- Repeated whitelist updates.
322	- Token balance invariants.
323	- Revocation and subsequent reapproval.
324	- Independent whitelist states across two deployed asset-token instances.
325	- A token whose issuer differs from the deploying account, simulating deployment by a future factory.
326	
327	Use meaningful test descriptions so failures are understandable.
328	
329	---
330	
331	## Step 4: Validate the Implementation
332	
333	After implementation:
334	
335	1. Compile all Solidity contracts.
336	2. Run the complete Phase 2 test suite.
337	3. Run any existing repository tests to detect regressions.
338	4. Fix all compilation errors and failing tests.
339	5. Check for common Solidity security problems.
340	6. Remove unnecessary code and unused imports.
341	7. Ensure code style matches the existing project.
342	8. Verify compatibility with the installed OpenZeppelin version.
343	
344	Run the actual relevant build and test commands, rather than merely describing what should be run.
345	
346	If existing failures are unrelated to Phase 2, document them without making unrelated changes.
347	
348	Do not claim any test passed unless you executed it successfully.
349	
350	---
351	
352	## Step 5: Documentation and AI Audit Evidence
353	
354	The SC4053 assignment requires an AI Audit Report evaluating AI-assisted development.
355	
356	Maintain an accurate and reviewable record of this phase.
357	
358	Create or update:
359	
360	`docs/phase2-implementation.md`
361	
362	Include:
363	
364	- Smart-contract overview.
365	- Explanation of ERC-20 tokenisation.
366	- Constructor parameters.
367	- Access-control architecture.
368	- Whitelist mechanism.
369	- Transfer restriction logic.
370	- Relevant functions and events.
371	- Explanation of the OpenZeppelin implementation choices.
372	- How Phase 3 will integrate with this contract.
373	- Testing methodology and outcomes.
374	
375	Also preserve evidence relevant to the AI Audit Report, using the existing documentation structure where possible.
376	
377	Record:
378	
379	1. The initial Phase 2 requirements.
380	2. How AI was used to generate or modify the implementation.
381	3. Major architectural decisions.
382	4. Any genuine bugs, security concerns or incorrect AI-generated code discovered.
383	5. Why each issue was problematic.
384	6. The actual fixes implemented.
385	7. Evidence demonstrating that the fixes work.
386	
387	Do not fabricate vulnerabilities or pretend tests were performed.
388	
389	If possible, preserve representative failing and passing tests for genuinely discovered issues.
390	
391	---
392	
393	## Step 6: Provide a Working Demonstration
394	
395	Create a minimal local demonstration using automated tests or a Hardhat script.
396	
397	The demonstration must prove the following:
398	
399	```text
400	1. Deploy Campus Property Token
401	   Name: Campus Property Token
402	   Symbol: CPT
403	   Supply: 10,000
404	
405	2. Verify:
406	   Issuer owns 10,000 CPT
407	
408	3. Whitelist Investor B
409	
410	4. Transfer 100 CPT:
411	   Issuer -> Investor B
412	
413	5. Verify:
414	   Issuer: 9,900 CPT
415	   Investor B: 100 CPT
416	
417	6. Attempt transfer:
418	   Investor B -> Unapproved Investor D
419	   Amount: 20 CPT
420	
421	7. Expected:
422	   Transaction REVERTED
423	
424	8. Whitelist Investor C
425	
426	9. Transfer:
427	   Investor B -> Investor C

# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 2: Asset Tokenisation and Compliance

## Project Context

We are developing a decentralised application (dApp) titled **Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum** for the NTU SC4053 Blockchain Technology Development Project.

The application simulates an institutional real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation platform, inspired by financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC.

Users will eventually be able to create tokenised assets, purchase tokens using testnet ETH, manage investor permissions, and transfer tokens between eligible wallets.

The project is being developed in six sequential phases:

1. Project Foundation and Architecture — COMPLETED
2. Asset Tokenisation and Compliance — CURRENT PHASE
3. Asset Registry and Primary Issuance
4. Frontend and MetaMask Integration
5. End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment
6. Security Audit, AI Evaluation and Final Submission

**Your task is to fully implement Phase 2, including Solidity development, automated testing, validation, and technical documentation.**

Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.

---

## Step 1: Inspect the Existing Repository

Before writing any code:

1. Read the existing README, project specifications, architecture documents, and relevant source files.
2. Inspect the Hardhat configuration, Solidity compiler version, OpenZeppelin version, package dependencies, and testing framework.
3. Understand the architecture established in Phase 1.
4. Identify any existing smart contracts or tests relevant to Phase 2.
5. Run the existing baseline tests, if available.
6. Preserve working Phase 1 code and established project conventions.

If there are minor differences between this prompt and the existing repository architecture, adapt the implementation to preserve compatibility. Document any meaningful architectural decisions.

Do not unnecessarily reinstall dependencies, overwrite configurations, introduce new frameworks, or restructure the project.

## Step 2: Implement `AssetToken.sol`

Create or complete:

`contracts/AssetToken.sol`

This is the core token contract representing fractional interests in a simulated real-world or digital asset.

### 2.1 ERC-20 Implementation

Use OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 implementation rather than writing token accounting from scratch.

The contract must support:

- Token name and symbol.
- Fixed initial token supply.
- Token balances.
- Standard `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom` functionality.
- ERC-20 `Transfer` and `Approval` events.
- Ownership records derived from token balances.

The contract constructor should accept:

```solidity
constructor(
    string memory name_,
    string memory symbol_,
    uint256 initialSupply_,
    address issuer_
)
```

Expected behaviour:

- The token name and symbol are configured at deployment.
- `initialSupply_` is minted to the issuer's wallet.
- `totalSupply()` returns the correct fixed supply.
- `balanceOf(issuer_)` initially equals `initialSupply_`.
- Token decimals are set to **0**, representing whole asset units.
- Further minting is not permitted after deployment.
- Zero issuer addresses and zero initial supply must be rejected.

For example:

```text
Token Name: Campus Property Token
Symbol: CPT
Initial Supply: 10,000
Decimals: 0

Issuer Balance: 10,000 CPT
Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
```

The MVP uses whole token units. Do not automatically multiply the supply by 10^18.

### 2.2 Role-Based Access Control

Implement role-based permissions using OpenZeppelin AccessControl.

At minimum, define:

```solidity
bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE =
    keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE");
```

The issuer supplied during deployment should initially receive:

- `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`
- `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`

The issuer must also automatically be whitelisted.

Only authorised compliance administrators may approve or revoke investor eligibility.

Important implementation detail: **Do not assume `msg.sender` is always the issuer during construction.**

In Phase 3, the token contract may be deployed by an asset factory on behalf of an issuer. Therefore, roles must be explicitly assigned to the `issuer_` constructor argument rather than blindly assigned to the deploying contract.

Do not implement the platform-wide issuer approval system yet; that belongs to Phase 3.

### 2.3 Investor Whitelisting

Implement an on-chain investor eligibility registry.

Suggested state variable:

```solidity
mapping(address => bool) public isWhitelisted;
```

Required function:

```solidity
function setWhitelisted(
    address investor,
    bool approved
) external;
```

Requirements:

1. Only addresses holding `COMPLIANCE_ROLE` may call the function.
2. Setting `approved = true` adds an investor to the whitelist.
3. Setting `approved = false` revokes an investor's eligibility.
4. Zero addresses cannot be whitelisted.
5. Emit a `WhitelistUpdated` event when eligibility changes.
6. Whitelist status must be publicly readable.

An approved investor is permitted to hold and receive the asset tokens.

An investor removed from the whitelist must no longer be able to send or receive tokens, even if they still have a positive token balance.

Do not forcibly confiscate or burn tokens when whitelist access is revoked.

### 2.4 Enforce Transfer Restrictions

This is the most important functionality of Phase 2.

Modify ERC-20 transfer behaviour so that tokens can only move between whitelisted addresses.

Expected behaviour:

| Sender | Recipient | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer succeeds |
| Whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
| Not whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
| Not whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |

**The restrictions must be enforced inside the token contract itself, not just in a separate purchasing contract or frontend.**

Both `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` must respect the restrictions.

If OpenZeppelin Contracts v5 is installed, use the appropriate ERC-20 `_update()` override to enforce transfer eligibility. If an older compatible version is already used by the project, implement the equivalent restriction using the supported hook for that version.

Do not downgrade OpenZeppelin or use deprecated methods just to follow an example.

Handle the zero-address minting case correctly during initial deployment.

The initial mint must succeed even though the zero address is not an eligible investor.

Avoid adding unnecessary restrictions to standard ERC-20 approval functionality unless required for security.

### 2.5 Contract Events and Errors

Implement clear events for compliance operations, such as:

```solidity
event WhitelistUpdated(
    address indexed investor,
    bool approved,
    address indexed operator
);
```

Use descriptive custom errors where appropriate.

The code should clearly distinguish failures caused by:

- Unauthorised compliance administration.
- Invalid wallet addresses.
- Non-whitelisted senders.
- Non-whitelisted recipients.
- Invalid constructor parameters.

Keep the implementation concise and readable.

### 2.6 Future Compatibility

The contract must be designed to support Phase 3 without major redesign.

In Phase 3, an `AssetSale` contract will temporarily hold token inventory and distribute tokens to approved investors.

Therefore:

- Compliance administrators must be able to whitelist smart-contract addresses, not only externally owned wallets.
- Whitelisted sale contracts must be capable of receiving and transferring asset tokens.
- The token should work when instantiated by a factory contract.
- The token must not depend on any frontend implementation.
- Each deployed token must maintain independent balances, roles, and whitelist state.

Do not implement `AssetSale.sol` or `AssetFactory.sol` in this phase.

---

## Step 3: Implement Automated Unit Tests

Create or update:

`test/AssetToken.test.js`

Use the testing framework already configured in Phase 1.

Tests must be deterministic and must not require Sepolia, MetaMask, live network access, or real ETH.

Use multiple local test accounts:

```text
Account A: Issuer / Compliance Admin
Account B: Approved Investor 1
Account C: Approved Investor 2
Account D: Unapproved Investor
Account E: Unauthorised Administrator
```

### Test Group A — Token Deployment

Verify:

1. Correct token name.
2. Correct token symbol.
3. Decimals equal 0.
4. Initial total supply equals 10,000.
5. Issuer initially receives 10,000 tokens.
6. Issuer is automatically whitelisted.
7. Issuer receives the required administrator roles.
8. Invalid issuer addresses are rejected.
9. Zero supply is rejected.
10. No externally accessible function can arbitrarily mint additional tokens.

### Test Group B — Investor Whitelisting

Verify:

1. Compliance admin can whitelist Account B.
2. Compliance admin can whitelist Account C.
3. Approved addresses return `true` from the whitelist.
4. Compliance admin can revoke Account B.
5. Revoked addresses return `false`.
6. Unauthorised Account E cannot whitelist investors.
7. Unauthorised Account E cannot revoke investors.
8. Whitelist modifications emit the expected event.
9. Attempts to whitelist the zero address revert.
10. Revoking a wallet does not silently change its token balance.

### Test Group C — ERC-20 Transfers

Test the following sequence:

1. Deploy CPT with 10,000 tokens.
2. Whitelist Account B.
3. Transfer 100 CPT from issuer to Account B.
4. Verify issuer balance equals 9,900.
5. Verify Account B balance equals 100.
6. Attempt transferring tokens from Account B to unapproved Account D.
7. Confirm the transaction reverts.
8. Verify all token balances remain unchanged after the revert.
9. Whitelist Account C.
10. Transfer 20 CPT from Account B to Account C.
11. Verify Account B now holds 80 CPT.
12. Verify Account C now holds 20 CPT.
13. Revoke Account B's whitelist status.
14. Verify Account B can neither send nor receive tokens.
15. Reapprove Account B.
16. Confirm transfers become possible again.

### Test Group D — Delegated Transfers

Test `approve()` and `transferFrom()`.

Verify:

- Allowances are created correctly.
- An approved delegated transfer between whitelisted holders succeeds.
- Delegated transfers to non-whitelisted recipients revert.
- Delegated transfers from non-whitelisted token holders revert.
- Failed delegated transfers do not unexpectedly alter balances or allowances.
- Standard ERC-20 insufficient-allowance behaviour is preserved.

Be careful not to confuse the spender with the actual token sender. Compliance checks must cover the token holder (`from`) and recipient (`to`).

### Test Group E — Edge Cases

Include tests for:

- Transfers exceeding the sender's balance.
- Transfers of zero tokens.
- Transfers to the zero address.
- Repeated whitelist updates.
- Token balance invariants.
- Revocation and subsequent reapproval.
- Independent whitelist states across two deployed asset-token instances.
- A token whose issuer differs from the deploying account, simulating deployment by a future factory.

Use meaningful test descriptions so failures are understandable.

---

## Step 4: Validate the Implementation

After implementation:

1. Compile all Solidity contracts.
2. Run the complete Phase 2 test suite.
3. Run any existing repository tests to detect regressions.
4. Fix all compilation errors and failing tests.
5. Check for common Solidity security problems.
6. Remove unnecessary code and unused imports.
7. Ensure code style matches the existing project.
8. Verify compatibility with the installed OpenZeppelin version.

Run the actual relevant build and test commands, rather than merely describing what should be run.

If existing failures are unrelated to Phase 2, document them without making unrelated changes.

Do not claim any test passed unless you executed it successfully.

---

## Step 5: Documentation and AI Audit Evidence

The SC4053 assignment requires an AI Audit Report evaluating AI-assisted development.

Maintain an accurate and reviewable record of this phase.

Create or update:

`docs/phase2-implementation.md`

Include:

- Smart-contract overview.
- Explanation of ERC-20 tokenisation.
- Constructor parameters.
- Access-control architecture.
- Whitelist mechanism.
- Transfer restriction logic.
- Relevant functions and events.
- Explanation of the OpenZeppelin implementation choices.
- How Phase 3 will integrate with this contract.
- Testing methodology and outcomes.

Also preserve evidence relevant to the AI Audit Report, using the existing documentation structure where possible.

Record:

1. The initial Phase 2 requirements.
2. How AI was used to generate or modify the implementation.
3. Major architectural decisions.
4. Any genuine bugs, security concerns or incorrect AI-generated code discovered.
5. Why each issue was problematic.
6. The actual fixes implemented.
7. Evidence demonstrating that the fixes work.

Do not fabricate vulnerabilities or pretend tests were performed.

If possible, preserve representative failing and passing tests for genuinely discovered issues.

---

## Step 6: Provide a Working Demonstration

Create a minimal local demonstration using automated tests or a Hardhat script.

The demonstration must prove the following:

```text
1. Deploy Campus Property Token
   Name: Campus Property Token
   Symbol: CPT
   Supply: 10,000

2. Verify:
   Issuer owns 10,000 CPT

3. Whitelist Investor B

4. Transfer 100 CPT:
   Issuer -> Investor B

5. Verify:
   Issuer: 9,900 CPT
   Investor B: 100 CPT

6. Attempt transfer:
   Investor B -> Unapproved Investor D
   Amount: 20 CPT

7. Expected:
   Transaction REVERTED

8. Whitelist Investor C

9. Transfer:
   Investor B -> Investor C
   Amount: 20 CPT

10. Verify final balances:
    Issuer: 9,900 CPT
    Investor B: 80 CPT
    Investor C: 20 CPT
    Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
```

This should run locally without requiring a connected wallet or deployed frontend.

---

## Step 7: Strict Scope Boundaries

This phase must implement only **asset tokenisation and compliance**.

Do not implement:

- Asset factory and asset registry.
- Primary token sale contracts.
- ETH payment functionality.
- Asset marketplaces.
- React frontend.
- MetaMask integration.
- Secondary-market trading.
- Price oracles.
- Dividend distribution.
- Token redemption.
- NFTs or ERC-721.
- Mainnet deployment.
- External KYC integrations.

Do not add unnecessary abstractions, upgradeable proxies, or complex external dependencies.

Focus on a clean, secure, well-tested implementation.

---

## Step 8: Final Acceptance Criteria

Phase 2 is complete only when:

- [ ] `AssetToken.sol` implements a working ERC-20 token.
- [ ] Tokens are minted correctly to the designated issuer.
- [ ] Total token supply is fixed.
- [ ] Token decimals are 0.
- [ ] Role-based administrative permissions work.
- [ ] Issuers/compliance administrators can whitelist investors.
- [ ] Unauthorised wallets cannot modify whitelist permissions.
- [ ] Only whitelisted wallets can send and receive tokens.
- [ ] Both `transfer` and `transferFrom` enforce restrictions.
- [ ] Revoked wallets cannot transfer tokens.
- [ ] Multiple independent token instances work.
- [ ] The full automated test suite passes.
- [ ] The demonstration scenario succeeds.
- [ ] Documentation is updated.
- [ ] AI-assisted development and any discovered issues are accurately documented.
- [ ] Existing Phase 1 functionality remains intact.

## Expected Final Response

Once implementation and testing are complete, provide a structured report containing:

**1. Files Created/Modified**
List every file changed and explain its purpose.

**2. Implementation Summary**
Explain what was built and the important contract-design decisions.

**3. Testing Results**
Provide the actual commands executed, number of tests passing/failing, and relevant terminal output.

**4. Security Considerations**
Describe access-control, whitelisting, transfer-restriction and supply-integrity protections.

**5. Issues Discovered**
Report any genuine errors encountered and how they were fixed.

**6. Phase 2 Completion Status**
State which acceptance criteria are satisfied and which, if any, remain incomplete.

**7. Phase 3 Readiness**
Explain how the finished `AssetToken` contract can integrate with the future asset factory and primary issuance contracts.

### Important Development Instructions

- Implement the functionality; do not stop after writing a plan.
- Inspect the repository before modifying files.
- Preserve Phase 1 architecture wherever possible.
- Prefer established OpenZeppelin implementations.
- Write and execute automated tests.
- Fix failures before finishing.
- Avoid unrelated changes.
- Do not make Git commits unless explicitly requested.
- Document assumptions and important deviations.
- Prioritise correct, secure, maintainable code over unnecessary functionality.

**Begin by inspecting the current repository, then complete Phase 2 from implementation through automated validation.**

1	# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 2: Asset Tokenisation and Compliance
2	
3	## Project Context
4	
5	We are developing a decentralised application (dApp) titled **Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum** for the NTU SC4053 Blockchain Technology Development Project.
6	
7	The application simulates an institutional real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation platform, inspired by financial institutions such as BlackRock, J.P. Morgan, and DTCC.
8	
9	Users will eventually be able to create tokenised assets, purchase tokens using testnet ETH, manage investor permissions, and transfer tokens between eligible wallets.
10	
11	The project is being developed in six sequential phases:
12	
13	1. Project Foundation and Architecture — COMPLETED
14	2. Asset Tokenisation and Compliance — CURRENT PHASE
15	3. Asset Registry and Primary Issuance
16	4. Frontend and MetaMask Integration
17	5. End-to-End Integration and Testnet Deployment
18	6. Security Audit, AI Evaluation and Final Submission
19	
20	**Your task is to fully implement Phase 2, including Solidity development, automated testing, validation, and technical documentation.**
21	
22	Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Step 1: Inspect the Existing Repository
27	
28	Before writing any code:
29	
30	1. Read the existing README, project specifications, architecture documents, and relevant source files.
31	2. Inspect the Hardhat configuration, Solidity compiler version, OpenZeppelin version, package dependencies, and testing framework.
32	3. Understand the architecture established in Phase 1.
33	4. Identify any existing smart contracts or tests relevant to Phase 2.
34	5. Run the existing baseline tests, if available.
35	6. Preserve working Phase 1 code and established project conventions.
36	
37	If there are minor differences between this prompt and the existing repository architecture, adapt the implementation to preserve compatibility. Document any meaningful architectural decisions.
38	
39	Do not unnecessarily reinstall dependencies, overwrite configurations, introduce new frameworks, or restructure the project.
40	
41	## Step 2: Implement `AssetToken.sol`
42	
43	Create or complete:
44	
45	`contracts/AssetToken.sol`
46	
47	This is the core token contract representing fractional interests in a simulated real-world or digital asset.
48	
49	### 2.1 ERC-20 Implementation
50	
51	Use OpenZeppelin's ERC-20 implementation rather than writing token accounting from scratch.
52	
53	The contract must support:
54	
55	- Token name and symbol.
56	- Fixed initial token supply.
57	- Token balances.
58	- Standard `transfer`, `approve`, `allowance`, and `transferFrom` functionality.
59	- ERC-20 `Transfer` and `Approval` events.
60	- Ownership records derived from token balances.
61	
62	The contract constructor should accept:
63	
64	```solidity
65	constructor(
66	    string memory name_,
67	    string memory symbol_,
68	    uint256 initialSupply_,
69	    address issuer_
70	)
71	```
72	
73	Expected behaviour:
74	
75	- The token name and symbol are configured at deployment.
76	- `initialSupply_` is minted to the issuer's wallet.
77	- `totalSupply()` returns the correct fixed supply.
78	- `balanceOf(issuer_)` initially equals `initialSupply_`.
79	- Token decimals are set to **0**, representing whole asset units.
80	- Further minting is not permitted after deployment.
81	- Zero issuer addresses and zero initial supply must be rejected.
82	
83	For example:
84	
85	```text
86	Token Name: Campus Property Token
87	Symbol: CPT
88	Initial Supply: 10,000
89	Decimals: 0
90	
91	Issuer Balance: 10,000 CPT
92	Total Supply: 10,000 CPT
93	```
94	
95	The MVP uses whole token units. Do not automatically multiply the supply by 10^18.
96	
97	### 2.2 Role-Based Access Control
98	
99	Implement role-based permissions using OpenZeppelin AccessControl.
100	
101	At minimum, define:
102	
103	```solidity
104	bytes32 public constant COMPLIANCE_ROLE =
105	    keccak256("COMPLIANCE_ROLE");
106	```
107	
108	The issuer supplied during deployment should initially receive:
109	
110	- `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`
111	- `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`
112	
113	The issuer must also automatically be whitelisted.
114	
115	Only authorised compliance administrators may approve or revoke investor eligibility.
116	
117	Important implementation detail: **Do not assume `msg.sender` is always the issuer during construction.**
118	
119	In Phase 3, the token contract may be deployed by an asset factory on behalf of an issuer. Therefore, roles must be explicitly assigned to the `issuer_` constructor argument rather than blindly assigned to the deploying contract.
120	
121	Do not implement the platform-wide issuer approval system yet; that belongs to Phase 3.
122	
123	### 2.3 Investor Whitelisting
124	
125	Implement an on-chain investor eligibility registry.
126	
127	Suggested state variable:
128	
129	```solidity
130	mapping(address => bool) public isWhitelisted;
131	```
132	
133	Required function:
134	
135	```solidity
136	function setWhitelisted(
137	    address investor,
138	    bool approved
139	) external;
140	```
141	
142	Requirements:
143	
144	1. Only addresses holding `COMPLIANCE_ROLE` may call the function.
145	2. Setting `approved = true` adds an investor to the whitelist.
146	3. Setting `approved = false` revokes an investor's eligibility.
147	4. Zero addresses cannot be whitelisted.
148	5. Emit a `WhitelistUpdated` event when eligibility changes.
149	6. Whitelist status must be publicly readable.
150	
151	An approved investor is permitted to hold and receive the asset tokens.
152	
153	An investor removed from the whitelist must no longer be able to send or receive tokens, even if they still have a positive token balance.
154	
155	Do not forcibly confiscate or burn tokens when whitelist access is revoked.
156	
157	### 2.4 Enforce Transfer Restrictions
158	
159	This is the most important functionality of Phase 2.
160	
161	Modify ERC-20 transfer behaviour so that tokens can only move between whitelisted addresses.
162	
163	Expected behaviour:
164	
165	| Sender | Recipient | Result |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| Whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer succeeds |
168	| Whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
169	| Not whitelisted | Whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
170	| Not whitelisted | Not whitelisted | Transfer reverts |
171	
172	**The restrictions must be enforced inside the token contract itself, not just in a separate purchasing contract or frontend.**
173	
174	Both `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` must respect the restrictions.
175	
176	If OpenZeppelin Contracts v5 is installed, use the appropriate ERC-20 `_update()` override to enforce transfer eligibility. If an older compatible version is already used by the project, implement the equivalent restriction using the supported hook for that version.
177	
178	Do not downgrade OpenZeppelin or use deprecated methods just to follow an example.
179	
180	Handle the zero-address minting case correctly during initial deployment.
181	
182	The initial mint must succeed even though the zero address is not an eligible investor.
183	
184	Avoid adding unnecessary restrictions to standard ERC-20 approval functionality unless required for security.
185	
186	### 2.5 Contract Events and Errors
187	
188	Implement clear events for compliance operations, such as:
189	
190	```solidity
191	event WhitelistUpdated(
192	    address indexed investor,
193	    bool approved,
194	    address indexed operator
195	);
196	```
197	
198	Use descriptive custom errors where appropriate.
199	
200	The code should clearly distinguish failures caused by:
201	
202	- Unauthorised compliance administration.
203	- Invalid wallet addresses.
204	- Non-whitelisted senders.
205	- Non-whitelisted recipients.
206	- Invalid constructor parameters.
207	
208	Keep the implementation concise and readable.
209	
210	### 2.6 Future Compatibility
211	
212	The contract must be designed to support Phase 3 without major redesign.
213	
214	In Phase 3, an `AssetSale` contract will temporarily hold token inventory and distribute tokens to approved investors.
215	
216	Therefore:
217	
218	- Compliance administrators must be able to whitelist smart-contract addresses, not only externally owned wallets.
219	- Whitelisted sale contracts must be capable of receiving and transferring asset tokens.
220	- The token should work when instantiated by a factory contract.
221	- The token must not depend on any frontend implementation.
222	- Each deployed token must maintain independent balances, roles, and whitelist state.
223	
224	Do not implement `AssetSale.sol` or `AssetFactory.sol` in this phase.
225	
226	---
227	
228	## Step 3: Implement Automated Unit Tests
229	
230	Create or update:
231	
232	`test/AssetToken.test.js`
233	
234	Use the testing framework already configured in Phase 1.
235	
236	Tests must be deterministic and must not require Sepolia, MetaMask, live network access, or real ETH.
237	
238	Use multiple local test accounts:
239	
240	```text
241	Account A: Issuer / Compliance Admin
242	Account B: Approved Investor 1
243	Account C: Approved Investor 2
244	Account D: Unapproved Investor
245	Account E: Unauthorised Administrator
246	```
247	
248	### Test Group A — Token Deployment
249	
250	Verify:
251	
252	1. Correct token name.
253	2. Correct token symbol.
254	3. Decimals equal 0.
255	4. Initial total supply equals 10,000.
256	5. Issuer initially receives 10,000 tokens.
257	6. Issuer is automatically whitelisted.
258	7. Issuer receives the required administrator roles.
259	8. Invalid issuer addresses are rejected.
260	9. Zero supply is rejected.
261	10. No externally accessible function can arbitrarily mint additional tokens.
262	
263	### Test Group B — Investor Whitelisting
264	
265	Verify:
266	
267	1. Compliance admin can whitelist Account B.
268	2. Compliance admin can whitelist Account C.
269	3. Approved addresses return `true` from the whitelist.
270	4. Compliance admin can revoke Account B.
271	5. Revoked addresses return `false`.
272	6. Unauthorised Account E cannot whitelist investors.
273	7. Unauthorised Account E cannot revoke investors.
274	8. Whitelist modifications emit the expected event.
275	9. Attempts to whitelist the zero address revert.
276	10. Revoking a wallet does not silently change its token balance.
277	
278	### Test Group C — ERC-20 Transfers
279	
280	Test the following sequence:
281	
282	1. Deploy CPT with 10,000 tokens.
283	2. Whitelist Account B.
284	3. Transfer 100 CPT from issuer to Account B.
285	4. Verify issuer balance equals 9,900.
286	5. Verify Account B balance equals 100.
287	6. Attempt transferring tokens from Account B to unapproved Account D.
288	7. Confirm the transaction reverts.
289	8. Verify all token balances remain unchanged after the revert.
290	9. Whitelist Account C.
291	10. Transfer 20 CPT from Account B to Account C.
292	11. Verify Account B now holds 80 CPT.
293	12. Verify Account C now holds 20 CPT.
294	13. Revoke Account B's whitelist status.
295	14. Verify Account B can neither send nor receive tokens.
296	15. Reapprove Account B.
297	16. Confirm transfers become possible again.
298	
299	### Test Group D — Delegated Transfers
300	
301	Test `approve()` and `transferFrom()`.
302	
303	Verify:
304	
305	- Allowances are created correctly.
306	- An approved delegated transfer between whitelisted holders succeeds.
307	- Delegated transfers to non-whitelisted recipients revert.
308	- Delegated transfers from non-whitelisted token holders revert.
309	- Failed delegated transfers do not unexpectedly alter balances or allowances.
310	- Standard ERC-20 insufficient-allowance behaviour is preserved.
311	
312	Be careful not to confuse the spender with the actual token sender. Compliance checks must cover the token holder (`from`) and recipient (`to`).
313	
314	### Test Group E — Edge Cases
315	
316	Include tests for:
317	
318	- Transfers exceeding the sender's balance.
319	- Transfers of zero tokens.
320	- Transfers to the zero address.
321	- Repeated whitelist updates.
322	- Token balance invariants.
323	- Revocation and subsequent reapproval.
324	- Independent whitelist states across two deployed asset-token instances.
325	- A token whose issuer differs from the deploying account, simulating deployment by a future factory.
326	
327	Use meaningful test descriptions so failures are understandable.
328	
329	---
330	
331	## Step 4: Validate the Implementation
332

options.description: Same precedent as Phase 2: add docs/spec/phase3-requirements.md + a note in spec-v1. authorizeIssuer/revokeIssuer/buyTokens/pricePerToken/assetToken, getAsset/getAssetCount. Test stub titles updated to match.

options.label: spec-v1 names govern
options.description: authoriseIssuer/deauthoriseIssuer/buy/priceWei/allocate as frozen; only add the Phase 3 extras (getAsset, getAssetCount, metadata, recovery).

options.label: Phase 3 names + spec-v1 aliases
options.description: Implement both name sets. More surface area to test and audit.

questions.question: What should createAsset take for metadata?

options.label: Strings for both (Recommended)
options.description: createAsset(name, symbol, description, assetType, supply, pricePerToken), assetType a free string like "Real Estate" / "Digital Licensing". Auto-incremented assetId.

options.label: assetType as enum
options.description: enum AssetType { RealWorld, Digital } — stricter, but the frontend must map it.

options.label: spec-v1 4-arg only
options.description: createAsset(name, symbol, supply, price); no description/assetType stored.

questions.question: How should unsold-inventory recovery work? (spec-v1 is silent; brief says 'if the sale is closed')

options.label: closeSale + recover (Recommended)
options.description: Issuer-only, irreversible closeSale(); afterwards buyTokens/allocate revert and issuer-only recoverUnsoldTokens() returns the sale's whole token balance to the issuer.

options.label: Recover any time
options.description: Issuer-only recoverUnsoldTokens(amount) callable while the sale is open; no closed state.

options.label: Out of scope
options.description: Skip recovery for Phase 3.

# SC4053 Blockchain Technology — Phase 3: Asset Registry and Primary Issuance

The text below is the user's Phase 3 request, given to Claude Code on 23 October 2026. Table formatting was lost when it was pasted and has been restored as Markdown; the wording is unchanged. The decisions in the final section were made by the user in the same session, in answer to questions raised by Claude Code about conflicts with `spec-v1.md`.

---

Deliverable: Functional on-chain asset issuance and purchase

Objective: Let authorised issuers create multiple tokenised assets and sell them to eligible investors.

This is where your project develops beyond a simple ERC-20 token demonstration.

## Task 3.1 — Implement AssetFactory.sol

The factory will act as the entry point for new asset issuance.

It should provide these functions:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `authorizeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin grants issuer permission |
| `revokeIssuer(address)` | Platform admin removes issuer creation permission |
| `createAsset(...)` | Authorised issuer creates an asset |
| `getAsset(assetId)` | Returns asset metadata and contract addresses |
| `getAssetCount()` | Returns number of registered assets |

A successful `createAsset()` should deploy an AssetToken and associated AssetSale, then record the asset in the registry.

Suggested metadata:

```text
assetId
name
symbol
description
assetType
totalSupply
tokenContract
saleContract
issuerAddress
unitPriceWei
```

The asset ID should be generated automatically rather than supplied by the issuer.

## Task 3.2 — Implement AssetSale.sol

This contract will facilitate primary-market purchases.

Essential variables:

```solidity
IERC20 public assetToken;
address public issuer;
uint256 public pricePerToken;
```

Main function:

```solidity
buyTokens(uint256 quantity) external payable
```

Purchase validation must confirm:

- The buyer is an approved investor.
- Quantity is greater than zero.
- Enough tokens remain in the sale contract.
- `msg.value` equals `quantity * pricePerToken`.

If every condition passes, the contract transfers tokens to the investor and records the purchase event.

Use exact payment for the MVP; partial payments, complex refunds and variable pricing are unnecessary.

## Task 3.3 — Implement the inventory funding process

The issuer must allocate tokens to the sale contract before buyers can purchase them.

The lifecycle will be:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Issuer creates an asset | 10,000 CPT minted to issuer |
| Issuer whitelists the sale contract | Contract is permitted to hold and transfer CPT |
| Issuer deposits 5,000 CPT for sale | Sale contract now has purchasable inventory |
| Investor buys 100 CPT | Investor pays 0.1 testnet ETH and receives 100 CPT |

To simplify the MVP, the price is fixed at asset creation. Later changes to the sale price are not supported.

## Task 3.4 — Implement issuer withdrawals

Create an issuer-only withdrawal function for sale proceeds.

The function must prevent unauthorised withdrawals and account for reentrancy risks when sending ETH. Include a protected way to recover any unsold token inventory if the sale is closed.

## Task 3.5 — Test factory and sale contracts

Test the following scenarios:

| Test case | Expected result |
|---|---|
| Unauthorised wallet creates an asset | Revert |
| Authorised issuer creates asset | Token and sale contracts deployed |
| Issuer creates two different assets | Both registered independently |
| Whitelisted investor buys 100 tokens | Correct ETH payment and token transfer |
| Investor underpays | Revert |
| Investor overpays | Revert |
| Investor buys more than inventory | Revert |
| Unapproved investor attempts purchase | Revert |
| Non-issuer withdraws proceeds | Revert |

Phase 3 completion criteria: From a Hardhat script or console, you should be able to register an issuer, create an asset, whitelist an investor, fund the sale contract, execute a purchase and inspect the updated balances.

You now have a working blockchain backend.

---

## Additional constraints from the session brief

- Implement AssetFactory and AssetSale only. Do not add pause, freeze or forced transfer to AssetToken in this phase; that needs a separate team decision.
- `withdrawProceeds` must follow checks-effects-interactions (spec-v1 §4 reentrancy requirement, invariant 8).
- `revokeIssuer` only blocks future `createAsset` calls. Contracts the issuer has already deployed keep operating (spec-v1 §5 note on `deauthoriseIssuer`).

## Decisions made by the user (23 October 2026)

Claude Code raised these conflicts between this request and `spec-v1.md` before writing code. The user chose:

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | spec-v1 and this request name functions and variables differently. Which governs? | **This request governs**, as Phase 2's requirements did. Use `authorizeIssuer`, `revokeIssuer`, `getAsset`, `getAssetCount`, `buyTokens`, `pricePerToken` and `assetToken`. spec-v1 names (`authoriseIssuer`, `deauthoriseIssuer`, `buy`, `priceWei`, `token`) are superseded. The test stub titles are updated to match. |
| D2 | What does `createAsset` take as metadata? | `createAsset(name, symbol, description, assetType, totalSupply, unitPriceWei)`. `assetType` is an enum: `AssetType { RealWorld, Digital }`. `assetId` is assigned automatically. |
| D3 | How is unsold inventory recovered? | An issuer-only, irreversible `closeSale()`. After closing, `buyTokens` and `allocate` revert, and an issuer-only `recoverUnsoldTokens()` returns the sale contract's entire token balance to the issuer. |
| D4 | The repo was mid-rebase of `fix/spec-corrections-phase1`. | Abort the rebase and merge the branch into `main` normally, so no published history is rewritten. |

# Phase 3 implementation: asset registry and primary issuance

Requirements: [phase3-requirements.md](spec/phase3-requirements.md), including user decisions D1–D4. Where those differ from [spec-v1](spec/spec-v1.md), they govern. Generated by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 23 October 2026. Commits are prefixed `ai:`.

## Contracts

### AssetFactory (`contracts/AssetFactory.sol`)

| Function | Caller | Reverts if | Event | Traces to |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `constructor(admin_)` | deployer | `admin_ == 0` (`InvalidAdmin`) | — | spec-v1 §4 |
| `authorizeIssuer(addr)` | admin | not admin (`NotAdmin`); `addr == 0`; already authorised | `IssuerAuthorised` | Phase 3 §3.1, spec-v1 §5 |
| `revokeIssuer(addr)` | admin | not admin; not authorised | `IssuerRevoked` | Phase 3 §3.1, spec-v1 §5 note |
| `createAsset(name, symbol, description, assetType, totalSupply, unitPriceWei)` | authorised issuer | not authorised; supply 0; price 0; bad enum value | `AssetCreated(assetId, token, sale, issuer)` | Phase 3 §3.1, D2 |
| `getAsset(assetId)` | anyone | unknown ID (`AssetNotFound`) | — | Phase 3 §3.1 |
| `getAssetCount()` | anyone | — | — | Phase 3 §3.1 |

- `assetId` is the registry index, starting at 0.
- `AssetType` is `{ RealWorld, Digital }` (D2).
- `authorisedIssuers` and `tokenToSale` keep their spec-v1 names. spec-v1's `address[] assets` is replaced by `getAsset` / `getAssetCount`.
- The factory is never granted a role on the tokens it deploys. Supply and both token roles go to the calling issuer, so the issuer must whitelist and fund the sale themselves (Phase 3 §3.3).
- Revoking an issuer only blocks future `createAsset` calls. Contracts already deployed keep working (spec-v1 §5 note; tested).

### AssetSale (`contracts/AssetSale.sol`)

| Function | Caller | Reverts if | Event | Traces to |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `allocate(amount)` | issuer | not issuer; closed; amount 0; sale not whitelisted; no allowance; insufficient balance | `Allocated` | Phase 3 §3.3, spec-v1 §5 |
| `buyTokens(quantity)` payable | whitelisted investor | closed; quantity 0; buyer not whitelisted; quantity > inventory; `msg.value != quantity * pricePerToken` | `Purchased(buyer, quantity, paid)` | Phase 3 §3.2 |
| `withdrawProceeds()` | issuer | not issuer; nothing owed; ETH send fails | `ProceedsWithdrawn` | Phase 3 §3.4, spec-v1 §4 reentrancy and invariant 8 |
| `closeSale()` | issuer | not issuer; already closed | `SaleClosed` | Phase 3 §3.4, D3 |
| `recoverUnsoldTokens()` | issuer | not issuer; sale open; no inventory | `UnsoldTokensRecovered` | Phase 3 §3.4, D3 |
| `availableTokens()` | anyone | — | — | spec-v1 §7 (investor dashboard) |

- `assetToken`, `issuer` and `pricePerToken` are `immutable`, so there is no way to change the price after creation (Phase 3 §3.3; tested).
- `assetToken` is typed `AssetToken` rather than the brief's `IERC20` because `buyTokens` must read `isWhitelisted`. The ABI is the same either way: an address getter.
- **Reentrancy (invariant 8):** proceeds are tracked in `unclaimedProceeds`. `withdrawProceeds` zeroes it before the `.call`.
- **No `receive`/`fallback`:** plain ETH sends revert, so ETH can only arrive through `buyTokens` and invariant 3 holds.
- `SafeERC20` is used for token movements, which is standard practice. AssetToken reverts on failure anyway.

## Tests

`npx hardhat test` → **99 passing, 0 pending, 0 failing.** Output: [test-full.log](evidence/phase3/test-full.log).

| Suite | Tests | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `test/AssetFactory.test.ts` | 18 | authorisation, creation, registry metadata, two independent assets, revocation scope, issuer isolation (invariant 7) |
| `test/AssetSale.test.ts` | 30 | allocation lifecycle, every Phase 3 §3.5 purchase case, proceeds, reentrancy (invariant 8), failed payout, close/recover (D3), invariants 1–3, the §3.3 lifecycle (10,000 / 5,000 / 100 CPT for 0.1 ETH) |
| AssetToken suites (Phase 2) | 51 | unchanged |

All nine Phase 3 §3.5 cases have a named test. The 22 placeholder stubs were replaced: titles were kept where still valid and renamed per D1.

**Mutation check for invariant 8.** The zeroing in `withdrawProceeds` was temporarily moved after the `.call`, the sale suite was re-run, and the file was restored with `git checkout`. Only the invariant 8 test failed (`expected 300000000000000000 to equal 0`). Output: [mutation-cei-withdraw.log](evidence/phase3/mutation-cei-withdraw.log). The harness (`contracts/test/AssetSaleIssuerHarness.sol`) records `unclaimedProceeds` from inside its `receive()` and asserts it is 0.

## Demo (completion criteria)

`npx hardhat run scripts/setupDemo.ts --network hardhatMainnet` runs these steps:

1. deploy the factory
2. authorise the issuer
3. create CPT and DLP
4. whitelist the CPT sale and the investor
5. allocate 5,000 CPT
6. investor buys 100 CPT for 0.1 ETH
7. print the balances: issuer 5,000 / sale 4,900 / investor 100 / supply 10,000 / sale ETH 0.1

Output: [setupDemo.log](evidence/phase3/setupDemo.log).

`scripts/deploy.ts` deploys the factory. On HTTP networks it also writes `frontend/src/config/addresses.json`. It has only been run in-process ([deploy-local.log](evidence/phase3/deploy-local.log)).

## AI mistakes observed in this session

These were caught before commit, in test code or test design, so no AUD issue was filed. Each is stated from what the session shows.

1. **Unsupported matcher chaining.** The first test draft chained `.emit(...).and.to.changeTokenBalances(...)`. The Hardhat 3 chai-matchers README lists `changeTokenBalances` as non-chainable. The run failed with an unhandled `ProviderError` ("maxFeePerGas … too low"). Both occurrences were split into separate `expect`s.
2. **An invariant 8 test that could not fail.** The first draft only checked that the re-entrant call did not succeed. That check passes even if the contract violates CEI: the sale only ever holds the ETH it owes, so a second payout fails for lack of funds whatever the ordering. This was found by reasoning, not by running the mutant against the weak test. It was fixed by asserting the balance seen mid-payout, then confirmed with the mutation above.

## Known limitations and open points

- **Factory size:** 22,557 bytes deployed with the optimiser off, against the EIP-170 limit of 24,576 ([bytecode-sizes.txt](evidence/phase3/bytecode-sizes.txt)). It fits, but little headroom remains. The `production` build profile enables the optimiser.
- **Standalone sales:** a standalone `AssetSale` can be deployed by anyone against any token. Its constructor does not check `issuer_ == token.issuer()`. The factory registry is the source of truth for legitimate sales. Such a contract can only sell inventory that its own "issuer" approved to it.
- **Whitelist dependencies:** the issuer can de-whitelist the sale contract, which halts buying and recovery. The issuer can also de-whitelist themselves, which blocks recovery. Both can be undone by the issuer, who holds `COMPLIANCE_ROLE`.
- **Sepolia demo:** `setupDemo.ts` needs three signers, but `hardhat.config.ts` configures one `PRIVATE_KEY` for Sepolia. Multi-wallet testnet runs belong to Phase 5.
- **No `localhost` network:** `hardhat.config.ts` defines no `localhost` network for a persistent `hardhat node`, which the Phase 4 frontend will need.
- **Out of scope:** pause, freeze and forced transfer (spec-v1 §4) are still not implemented, pending a team decision. AUD-001 stays open for them.
- **`scripts/evidence.sh` was not run.** It requires `forge`, which this Hardhat project does not use.

content.text:
Phase 3 is done and committed to local `main`. `npx hardhat test` gives **99 passing, 0 pending, 0 failing** (the 51 existing AssetToken tests plus 48 new factory and sale tests). Nothing is pushed.

**Git cleanup first.** The interactive rebase of `fix/spec-corrections-phase1` was aborted. OneDrive left a lock on git's rebase folder, which I removed by hand. I then merged the branch into `main` normally (`404b75a`), resolving `.gitignore` to `types/ethers-contracts/` and keeping both rows in `INDEX.md`. That merge brings in the spec corrections your brief relied on (Invariant 8 and the deauthorise scope note), which hadn't been on main before. It also includes `33d4e25`, the session-transcript commit that had never been pushed.

**Commits on main, in order:**
- `docs:` `docs/spec/phase3-requirements.md` holds your brief plus your decisions D1–D4, and spec-v1 now points to it.
- `ai:` `AssetFactory.sol` and `AssetSale.sol`, written to your decisions:
  - Phase 3 function names.
  - An `AssetType` enum.
  - `closeSale()` then `recoverUnsoldTokens()` for unsold inventory.
  - `withdrawProceeds` sets the owed balance to zero before sending ETH, as Invariant 8 requires.
- `ai:` the tests cover every case in the Task 3.5 table, invariants 1–3, 7 and 8, and the recovery flow. They use a test contract that acts as the issuer and tries to re-enter `withdrawProceeds`.
- `ai:` `deploy.ts` and `setupDemo.ts`. The demo meets the completion criteria end to end: issuer 5,000 / sale 4,900 / investor 100 CPT, with 0.1 ETH in the sale contract.
- `evidence:` logs are in `docs/evidence/phase3/`.
- `docs:` `docs/phase3-implementation.md`, follow-ups on AUD-001 and AUD-003, and an AI-log row.

**Audit-relevant points (all in `phase3-implementation.md`):**
- **My first draft of the Invariant 8 test could never fail.** The sale only holds the ETH it owes, so a second payout fails for lack of funds whatever order the code runs in. I made the test check the owed balance during the payout. Then I moved the zeroing after the ETH send, ran the tests, and confirmed only that test failed. The file was restored afterwards.
- **One test-code bug:** I chained balance-change checks in a way Hardhat 3 doesn't support. It was fixed before commit. No AUD issues were filed because no committed contract code was wrong.
- **The factory is close to the contract size limit:** 22,557 of 24,576 bytes with the optimiser off.
- **Your brief had two errors:** there were 12 AssetSale stubs, not 22, and Invariant 8 wasn't on main yet.

**Still open:**
- Pause, freeze and forced transfer were left out as you instructed, so AUD-001 stays open for them.
- `evidence.sh` wasn't run because it needs `forge`.
- No Sepolia deploy has been attempted. The Sepolia config has one wallet, but the demo needs three.
- No `localhost` network is defined, which the Phase 4 frontend will need.
- The transcript export for this session is marked pending in the AI-log index.

Everything checked out, so I pushed `main` and deleted the local `fix/spec-corrections-phase1` branch.

**Checks before pushing:**
- **Git state:** the working tree was clean, and origin/main had no commits that local main lacked, so the push was a plain fast-forward.
- **Secrets:** no `.env` file is tracked, and `.env.example` holds empty placeholders only. Nothing in the 13 pushed commits looks like a private key or an RPC/API key.
- **Build and tests:** a clean build compiled all 5 contracts with no warnings, and `npx hardhat test` gave 99 passing, 0 pending, 0 failing.
- **Scripts:** `setupDemo.ts` again showed issuer 5,000 / sale 4,900 / investor 100 CPT, total supply 10,000, and 0.1 ETH held by the sale. `deploy.ts` deployed the factory.
- **Tags:** `spec-v0` wasn't touched, and no `ai-baseline` branch or tag was created.

**Push:** `e3d0cc4..7fd3e26` on `origin/main`. Origin had been further behind than I thought, so this push also published the earlier merge commit `7af22c9`, the fix-branch commits, and the transcript export `33d4e25`, which had never been pushed.

**Branch deletion:** `git branch -d` refused because `33d4e25` isn't on `origin/fix/spec-corrections-phase1`.
